title: 3,000 Matchlocks Firing in Turns? Did Nagashino's "Three-Row Volley" Really Happen?
description:
Tenshō 3, 5th month, 21st day (June 29, 1575 in the Julian calendar; July 9 in the Gregorian): at Nagashino in Mikawa, Oda and Tokugawa ashigaru crouch behind wooden fences built to stop horses, and across the field the Takeda army beats the drums to attack. For many people, the next picture is 3,000 matchlocks lined up in three rows, firing in turns: the "three-row volley" (sandan-uchi).

This episode follows that picture layer by layer, in the order the records were written: Ōta Gyūichi's Shinchō Kōki only says "about 1,000 matchlocks," and the side that came on in turns was the Takeda; in the early Edo period, Oze Hoan's Shinchōki (usually dated to 1622, Genna 8, with 1604 and 1611 also proposed) makes it 3,000, a thousand per round, yet writes the last wave as a single all-out volley; 17th-century genealogies and war tales add "in turns" and "three relays" (mitsugawari); and in 1903 (Meiji 36) the Army General Staff's Nihon Senshi: Nagashino-eki adds "3,000 picked from 10,000 gunners in the whole army." Finally: how researchers have questioned it since 1980, and the Ikeda family copy and the folding screens that no one has yet checked in person.

The Shinchō Kōki is quoted from the Meiji-era Wagajikan Wagasho edition on Wikisource; Hoan's Shinchōki from the Genna 8 old movable-type edition, and the Nihon Senshi: Nagashino-eki from the 1903 edition, both in the National Diet Library Digital Collections. Most of the research history is secondhand, and each such source is marked in the references below.

The source of every quotation, year and number is listed in the references below; dates in the narration follow the old lunar calendar, and sentences beginning "we think" are this channel's view.

The illustrations in this episode are AI-generated; the historical figures in them are cartoon characters, unnamed and not meant as likenesses; modern researchers are not depicted.

Data as of 2026-10-19

chapters.dawn-fence: Tenshō 3, dawn: the matchlocks wait behind the fence
chapters.ota-writes: Ōta Gyūichi only wrote: about 1,000 matchlocks
chapters.hoan-intro: Forty-odd years later, Hoan makes it 3,000
chapters.genealogy: Genealogies add turns; the General Staff picks 3,000

ng101.text: Tenshō 3, 5th month, 21st day: Nagashino, in Mikawa.

ng102.text: Behind anti-horse fences, ashigaru crouch with matchlocks; opposite, Takeda drums beat.

ng103.text: By the standard answer of 100-plus years, he'll now join one of three rows:

ng104.text: Front row fires, falls back to reload, next row steps in—repeat.

ng105.text: Later it was named the "three-row volley."

ng106.text: The first book to record this day also mentions the number "3,000." Where?

ng107.text: That morning, an army really was coming on in turns.

ng108.text: Forty-odd years on, another man wrote up this battle. In the last wave, what did his matchlocks do?

ng109.text: In Meiji 36, the Army General Staff added one more number to it.

ng110.text: That morning, how exactly did the matchlocks behind the fence fire?

ng201.text: First to record it: Ōta Gyūichi's Shinchō Kōki.

ng202.text: What he wrote: matchlocks, about a thousand.

ng204.text: They went to five commanders, who sent ashigaru inching toward the enemy.

ng207.text: 500 more crossed the river at night with a unit,

ng209.text: Nobunaga's roughly 30,000 men were hidden tier by tier in hollows, out of sight.

ng210.text: The Kōki's "tiers" are about hiding troops, not firing.

ng211.text: The Takeda had only about half as many men.

ng212.text: At daybreak, the first Takeda wave charged, drums beating.

ng213.text: The first wave pulled back, the second came on; then the third, fourth and fifth.

ng214.text: That army coming on in turns—which side was it?

ng216.text: Gyūichi writes: from sunrise into afternoon, wave after wave.

ng217.text: Third wave: Kantō men, fine riders, set on charging in on horseback.

ng219.text: Not one main unit went out; just matchlocks and ashigaru.

ng220.text: The ashigaru behind the fence? Gyūichi writes: they hid, waiting for the enemy.

ng222.text: He also notes: when the enemy charged, fall back; when it retreated, follow.

ng223.text: Read the whole passage: no groups, no swapping, no firing in turns.

ng224.text: By afternoon the Takeda withdrew, many senior vassals lost.

ng225.text: So, that opening question: where in Gyūichi's book is "3,000"?

ng226.text: Five years before Nagashino: Genki 1, the fighting at Noda and Fukushima.

ng227.text: Some 20,000 men from Kii, the Negoro and Saika among them, reportedly brought exactly that many guns.

ng228.text: Back then, they came to fight on Oda's side.

ng229.text: For Gyūichi, those were someone else's guns. Who moved the number to Nagashino?

ng301.text: The man who moved it was Oze Hoan.

ng302.text: In early Edo, 40-odd years after the battle, his Shinchōki was printed.

ng303.text: Gyūichi's book stayed in manuscript; Hoan's was printed and spread far wider.

ng304.text: Yet a Tokugawa retainer of the same era wrote that it was full of lies.

ng305.text: Hoan writes first: Katsuyori's men were all fine riders, so fences were built.

ng306.text: Gyūichi's fine riders were just the third wave; with Hoan, they became the whole army.

ng307.text: Then the opening number appears: matchlocks drawn from every unit, 3,000,

ng308.text: handed to the same five commanders.

ng309.text: The order: no firing until the enemy is within about 100 meters.

ng310.text: Then: a thousand fire at a time, tier by tier, taking turns.

ng312.text: Not in the book; readers did that math.

ng313.text: Remember Gyūichi: they charge, fall back; they go, follow?

ng314.text: Hoan's passage is reworked from it, plus that line about turns.

ng315.text: Here's the problem: within one book, the number itself wobbles.

ng316.text: First it's 3,000, a thousand per round; later, 3,000 at a time, taking turns.

ng317.text: Tokugawa's 300 matchlock ashigaru fight another way: each reloads and keeps firing.

ng318.text: In the fifth wave, Takeda's last unit charged.

ng319.text: Remember his matchlocks in the last wave?

ng320.text: Hoan writes: as the enemy closed in, over 2,000 matchlocks fired all at once.

ng321.text: The "three" that Hoan never wrote—who wrote it in later?

ng401.text: Before the "three," a genealogy changed one thing.

ng402.text: This 1640s genealogy of daimyo has Hoan's gun count,

ng403.text: but it says: the five commanders gave orders in turns.

ng404.text: What rotates is the commanders, not the guns.

ng405.text: Then the late-17th-century Sōkenki puts it outright:

ng406.text: a thousand a turn, three turns.

ng407.text: That's the earliest place we found the "three" spelled out.

ng408.text: In Meiji 36, the Army General Staff published Nihon Senshi: Nagashino-eki.

ng410.text: 10,000 gunners in the whole army, 3,000 picked from them.

ng411.text: Gyūichi never wrote these 10,000. Nor did Hoan.

ng412.text: The orders follow suit: each thousand fires in turn.

ng413.text: Stranger still, its appendix quotes a Takeda military manual:

ng414.text: The horses charging the fence are a lie; ten horses couldn't ride abreast at Nagashino.

ng415.text: But Gyūichi's third wave clearly charged on horseback. The two don't match.

ng416.text: And the opening picture—front row fires, falls back to reload? In this book?

ng417.text: No. Not even the General Staff wrote that.

ng418.text: Researchers found the step-back-and-reload layer was added after the Nihon Senshi.

ng419.text: Historian Tokutomi Sohō copied it into his own big history; prewar scholars said the same.

ng420.text: The "standard answer of over a century" counts from this very book.

ng421.text: A Japanese high-school textbook today says matchlock units beat Takeda's cavalry; no "three rows."

ng422.text: 70-odd years on, someone finally asked a question. What was it?

ng501.text: In 1980, researcher Fujimoto Masayuki wrote an article, its title blunt: Nagashino's matchlock tactics are fiction.

ng502.text: He asked: who, standing where, how, could keep calling volleys for that many gunners?

ng503.text: His answer: it can't be done. Takeda lost, above all, on numbers.

ng504.text: Three men a group, firing in turns—does it work?

ng505.text: Someone tested a matchlock: one man loading and firing alone, about 20 seconds a shot.

ng506.text: Three men taking turns, same six shots: roughly three times faster. Firing in turns works.

ng507.text: But a man who fires matchlocks at old battlefield shows says: in some corner, maybe;

ng508.text: a whole 2-km line firing on command, with enough ammo? He can't picture it.

ng509.text: One copy of the Shinchō Kōki has a tiny "three" above and right of "thousand."

ng511.text: Some say this copy is in Gyūichi's own hand.

ng512.text: That "three" is widely seen as added later; or his own fix.

ng514.text: And the Edo-period Nagashino battle screens—what do they show?

ng515.text: The museums say: fences, matchlock units, and mounted warriors charging in.

ng516.text: A report says they show no three-row volley. But a painting can't show rows rotating;

ng517.text: We haven't seen these screens in person.

ng518.text: We think this picture has lasted so long because it turned a murky victory into one tidy diagram.

ng519.text: Remember the three rows added layer by layer? Drawn later, yes; but that can't prove no one fired in turns that day.

ng521.text: Where did you first see three rows taking turns?

ng522.text: This channel tells only what records hold; subscribe to open files with us.
